title: 25 States Sue Trump Administration Over Latest Round of Global Tariffs
excerpt: Democratic attorneys general argue the president's Section 301 tariffs on 60 trading partners, including India, exceed his legal authority and hurt consumers.
body:
• Twenty-five Democratic-led states filed suit in the U.S. Court of International Trade on Monday to block tariffs of 10%–12.5% on goods from 60 countries.
  • The tariffs, imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, target nations the White House says fail to enforce bans on forced-labor imports — covering 99% of all U.S. imports.
  • India is among the 54 countries facing the higher 12.5% tariff rate, raising costs for goods ranging from spices to textiles.
  • The lawsuit follows the Supreme Court's February ruling that struck down Trump's earlier IEEPA-based tariffs as exceeding presidential authority.

The Lawsuit

A coalition of 25 states, all led by Democratic attorneys general or governors, filed a lawsuit on Monday challenging the Trump administration's latest tariffs on imports from 60 trading partners. The states argue the president's team rushed through legally required investigations and failed to demonstrate that the new levies will effectively combat forced labor in global supply chains.

https://x.com/CNBC/status/2084426181185622155

The suit was filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade in New York, the same venue where previous tariff challenges have landed. Oregon and New York are among the states leading the effort.

"Instead, the administration is using 'forced labor' as an excuse to continue its policy of indiscriminately enacting damaging tariffs on a wide range of countries."

— Letitia James, New York Attorney General

Oregon's Attorney General Dan Rayfield was blunt in his assessment. "Despite losing every step of the way, Trump is trying yet again to inflict more chaos on working families and homegrown Oregon businesses," he said in a statement.

What the Tariffs Cover

The Trump administration on July 24 imposed the new tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, accusing 60 nations of not doing enough to curb the export of goods produced with forced labor. The tariffs replaced a temporary 10% global tariff that had expired.

The rates split into two tiers: 10% for countries including Canada, the European Union, Mexico, and Taiwan, and 12.5% for nations including China, Japan, South Korea, and India. Together, the affected nations account for 99.4% of all U.S. imports, according to the U.S. Trade Representative's office.

India lands in the higher bracket alongside 53 other countries that the USTR found had "failed to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor." The designation covers a sweeping range of Indian exports to the U.S., from pharmaceuticals and textiles to agricultural products and IT hardware.

Legal Landscape

The states' challenge follows a series of legal setbacks for the administration's tariff agenda. In February, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) did not authorize the president to unilaterally impose broad tariffs on trading partners. The Court of International Trade also ruled against temporary replacement tariffs, though those expired before an appeals court could weigh in.

In response, the administration pivoted to Section 301, a more established trade remedy tool that presidents have used since the 1970s. Trade lawyers have noted that courts have historically given the executive branch more leeway under this provision, meaning the states' lawsuit could face longer odds than previous challenges.

White House spokesman Kush Desai defended the approach. "Section 301 tariffs have proven to be a legally durable tool since the President's first term, and they remain so now," he said.

Small businesses have also challenged the tariffs. Spice importer Burlap & Barrel and watch retailer Collective Horology filed a separate lawsuit on the day the tariffs took effect, represented by the Liberty Justice Center.

What It Means for Indian Businesses and the Diaspora

For Indian exporters and diaspora-owned businesses with supply chains running through India, the 12.5% tariff adds a fresh layer of cost pressure. Indian spice importers, textile distributors, and IT hardware resellers operating in the U.S. face higher landed costs on inventory — costs that typically flow through to consumers.

The timing compounds existing trade friction. India's generic pharmaceutical exports to the U.S., already under scrutiny from Trump's pharma tariff agenda, now carry an additional Section 301 surcharge. Remittance flows and bilateral trade volumes, which reached $130 billion in 2025, could face headwinds if the tariffs remain in place.

What's Next

The legal timeline remains uncertain. Previous tariff cases have moved through the courts over months, and the administration has continued imposing new tariffs even as earlier ones were struck down. USTR Jamieson Greer said the agency is also pursuing a separate Section 301 investigation targeting excess industrial capacity in 16 key trading partners, including China, Vietnam, and Mexico, which could lead to additional tariffs.

For now, the 10%–12.5% tariffs remain in effect. Markets will be watching whether the Court of International Trade grants any preliminary relief — and whether the Supreme Court eventually weighs in on the limits of Section 301 authority.
